paragraphs: What the Real Advantages Are That American Society Derives from the Government of the Democracy

Before I begin the subject of this chapter, I want to remind the reader of something I have mentioned more than once in this book. The political institutions of the United States seem to me one of the forms of government that a democracy may adopt, but I do not regard the American Constitution as the best, or as the only one, that a democratic people may establish. In showing the advantages the Americans draw from the government of the democracy, I am therefore very far from meaning, or believing, that the same advantages can be obtained only from the same laws.
General Tendency of the Laws Under the Rule of the American Democracy, and the Habits of Those Who Apply Them

The defects of a democratic government are easy to discover—Its advantages can be seen only through long observation—Democracy in America is often inexpert, but the general tendency of its laws is beneficial—In the American democracy, public officials have no permanent interests distinct from those of the majority—The result of this state of things.

The defects and weaknesses of a democratic government are very easy to discover. The most glaring examples demonstrate them, while its beneficial influence works less visibly. A single glance is enough to detect its bad consequences, but its good qualities can be seen only through long observation. The laws of the American democracy are often defective or incomplete. They sometimes attack vested rights, or give approval to others that are dangerous to the community. But even if they were good, the frequent changes they undergo would be an evil. How is it, then, that the American republics prosper and hold their position?

In judging laws, we must carefully distinguish between the end at which they aim and the means by which they pursue that end, between their absolute and their relative excellence. Suppose a legislator intends to favor the interests of the minority at the expense of the majority, and suppose the measures he takes are so arranged that they accomplish his object with the least possible expense of time and effort. Then the law may be well drafted even though its purpose is bad, and the more effective it is, the greater the harm it does.

Democratic laws generally tend to promote the welfare of the greatest possible number. They come from the majority of the citizens, who may make mistakes but cannot have an interest opposed to their own advantage. The laws of an aristocracy, on the contrary, tend to concentrate wealth and power in the hands of the minority, because an aristocracy, by its very nature, is a minority. We may therefore state as a general proposition that a democracy, in conducting its legislation, aims at something useful to a greater number of citizens than an aristocracy does. This, however, is the sum total of its advantages.

Aristocracies are infinitely more expert in the science of legislation than democracies can ever be. They possess a self-control that protects them from the errors of momentary excitement, and they form lasting designs that they bring to maturity with the help of favorable opportunities. Aristocratic government proceeds with the skill of an art; it knows how to make the combined force of all its laws converge on a given point at the same time. This is not so with democracies, whose laws are almost always ineffective or ill-timed. The means of a democracy are therefore more imperfect than those of an aristocracy, and the measures it adopts without realizing it are often opposed to its own cause. But the object it has in view is more useful.

Now imagine a community so organized, by nature or by its constitution, that it can endure the passing effects of bad laws and can wait, without being destroyed, for the general tendency of its legislation to show itself. We can then understand that a democratic government, in spite of its defects, will be best suited to promote the prosperity of such a community. This is precisely what has happened in the United States. And I repeat what I have said before: the great advantage of the Americans is that they can commit faults which they are able to repair afterward.

A similar observation can be made about public officials. It is easy to see that the American democracy often errs in choosing the individuals to whom it entrusts the power of administration, but it is harder to say why the State prospers under their rule. In the first place, we should note that if the governors in a democratic State have less honesty and less ability than elsewhere, the governed, on the other hand, are better informed and pay closer attention to their interests. Because the people in democracies are more constantly vigilant in their affairs and more jealous of their rights, they keep their representatives from abandoning the general line of conduct that their own interest prescribes. In the second place, we must remember that although the democratic magistrate is more likely to abuse his power, he holds it for a shorter time. But there is yet another reason, more general and more conclusive. It is no doubt important to the welfare of nations that they be governed by men of talent and virtue. But it is perhaps still more important that the interests of those men not differ from the interests of the community at large. For if they did, high virtues might become useless and talents might be put to bad use. I say it is important that the interests of the persons in authority not conflict with or oppose the interests of the community at large. I do not insist that they be the same as the interests of the whole population, because I know of no country where that has ever been the case.

No political form has yet been found that is equally good for the prosperity and development of every class into which society is divided. These classes remain, as it were, a number of separate nations inside one nation. Experience has shown that it is just as dangerous to leave the fate of these classes entirely in the hands of any one of them as it is to make one people the judge of another’s destiny. When the rich alone govern, the interest of the poor is always at risk, and when the poor make the laws, the rich face very serious dangers. So the advantage of democracy does not lie, as some have claimed, in promoting the prosperity of everyone, but simply in serving the well-being of the greatest possible number.

The men entrusted with directing public affairs in the United States are often inferior, both in ability and in morality, to those whom aristocratic institutions would raise to power. But their interest is identified and bound up with that of the majority of their fellow citizens. They may often be faithless and often mistaken, but they will never systematically adopt a line of conduct opposed to the will of the majority, and it is impossible for them to give the government a dangerous or exclusive tendency.

The misadministration of a democratic magistrate is a purely isolated fact, which occurs only during the short period for which he is elected. Corruption and incapacity are not common interests that can connect men permanently with one another. A corrupt or incapable magistrate will not coordinate his measures with another magistrate merely because that person is as corrupt and as incapable as himself. And these two men will never join their efforts to promote the corruption and incompetence of their distant descendants. On the contrary, the ambition and scheming of one will serve to expose the other. In democratic states, the vices of a magistrate are usually particular to his own person.

But under aristocratic governments, public men are swayed by the interest of their order. That interest is sometimes the same as the interests of the majority, but it is very often distinct from them. It is the common and lasting bond that unites these men. It leads them to join together and combine their efforts to reach an end that does not always secure the greatest happiness of the greatest number. And it serves not only to connect the persons in authority but to unite them with a considerable part of the community, since many citizens belong to the aristocracy without holding official positions. The aristocratic magistrate is therefore constantly supported by a part of the community, as well as by the government of which he is a member.

The common purpose that links the interest of the magistrates in aristocracies with that of a portion of their contemporaries also identifies it with that of future generations. Their influence belongs to the future as much as to the present. The aristocratic magistrate is urged toward the same point at once by the passions of the community, by his own, and, I might almost add, by those of his descendants. Is it any wonder, then, that he does not resist such repeated impulses? Indeed, aristocracies are often carried away by the spirit of their order without being corrupted by it, and they unconsciously shape society to their own ends and prepare it for their own descendants.

The English aristocracy is perhaps the most liberal that has ever existed, and no body of men has ever supplied, without interruption, so many honorable and educated individuals to the government of a country. Yet it cannot escape notice that in English legislation the good of the poor has been sacrificed to the advantage of the rich, and the rights of the majority to the privileges of the few. As a result, England today combines the extremes of fortune within her society, and her perils and calamities are almost equal to her power and her renown. *a

a [ [English legislation over the past forty years is certainly not fairly open to this criticism, which was written before the Reform Bill of 1832. Accordingly, Great Britain has so far escaped and overcome the perils and calamities to which she seemed to be exposed.]]

In the United States, public officials have no interests to promote that are tied to a caste, and the general and constant influence of the government is beneficial, even though the individuals who carry it on are often unskillful and sometimes contemptible. There is indeed a hidden tendency in democratic institutions to make the efforts of the citizens serve the prosperity of the community, in spite of their private vices and mistakes. In aristocratic institutions, by contrast, there is a hidden inclination that leads those who conduct the government, despite their talents and virtues, to contribute to the evils that oppress their fellow creatures. In aristocratic governments, public men may often do harm they do not intend, and in democratic states they produce benefits they never thought of.
Public Spirit in the United States

Patriotism of instinct—Patriotism of reflection—Their different characteristics—Nations ought to strive to acquire the second when the first has disappeared—The efforts of the Americans toward this end—The interest of the individual is closely connected with that of the country.

There is one kind of patriotic attachment that arises mainly from an instinctive, disinterested, and undefinable feeling that ties a man’s affections to his birthplace. This natural fondness goes together with a taste for ancient customs and a reverence for the traditions of the past. Those who feel it love their country as they love the house of their fathers. They enjoy the tranquillity it affords them. They cling to the peaceful habits they have formed within it. They are attached to the memories it awakens, and they are even pleased by the state of obedience in which they live. This patriotism is sometimes stirred up by religious enthusiasm, and then it is capable of the most prodigious efforts. It is in itself a kind of religion. It does not reason, but acts from the impulse of faith and feeling. Some nations have regarded the monarch as the embodiment of the country. The fervor of patriotism was then turned into the fervor of loyalty, and they took a sympathetic pride in his conquests and gloried in his power. At one time, under the ancient monarchy, the French felt a kind of satisfaction in their dependence on the arbitrary pleasure of their king, and they used to say with pride, “We are the subjects of the most powerful king in the world.”

But like all instinctive passions, this kind of patriotism is better at prompting short bursts of effort than at supplying the motives for continuous endeavor. It may save the State in a crisis, but it will often let the nation decline in time of peace. As long as the customs of a people are simple and its faith unshaken, as long as society rests steadily on traditional institutions whose legitimacy has never been questioned, this instinctive patriotism tends to last.

But there is another kind of attachment to a country that is more rational than the one we have just described. It is perhaps less generous and less ardent, but it is more fruitful and more lasting. It arises together with the spread of knowledge, it is nourished by the laws, it grows through the exercise of civil rights, and in the end it merges with the personal interest of the citizen. A man understands the influence that his country’s prosperity has on his own welfare. He knows that the laws allow him to contribute to that prosperity, and he works to promote it, first as a part of his interest and second as a part of his right.

But there are times in the life of a nation when the ancient customs of a people are changed, public morality is destroyed, religious belief is disturbed, and the spell of tradition is broken, while the spread of knowledge is still incomplete and the civil rights of the community are poorly secured or confined within very narrow limits. The country then takes on a dim and uncertain shape in the eyes of its citizens. They no longer see it in the soil they live on, for to them that soil is a dull, lifeless clod. They do not see it in the usages of their forefathers, which they have been taught to regard as a degrading yoke. They do not see it in religion, for of that they doubt. They do not see it in the laws, which do not originate in their own authority, nor in the legislator, whom they fear and despise. The country is lost to their senses. They can discover it neither under its own features nor under borrowed ones, and they shut themselves up within the dull confines of a narrow egotism. They are freed from prejudice without having acknowledged the empire of reason. They are moved neither by the instinctive patriotism of monarchical subjects nor by the thinking patriotism of republican citizens. They have stopped halfway between the two, in the midst of confusion and distress.

In this predicament, retreat is impossible. A people can no more recover the vitality of its earlier times than a man can return to the innocence and bloom of childhood. Such things may be regretted, but they cannot be renewed. The only thing left to do, then, is to go forward and hasten the union of private with public interests, since the period of disinterested patriotism has gone by forever.

I am certainly very far from claiming that, to obtain this result, the exercise of political rights should immediately be granted to all members of the community. But I maintain that the most powerful means we still possess of interesting men in the welfare of their country, and perhaps the only one, is to make them partakers in the government. At the present time, civic zeal seems to me inseparable from the exercise of political rights. And I hold that the number of citizens in Europe will be found to grow or shrink in proportion as those rights are extended.

In the United States the inhabitants were set down on the soil they now occupy only yesterday, as it were. They brought neither customs nor traditions with them. They meet one another for the first time with no previous acquaintance. In short, the instinctive love of country can scarcely exist in their minds. Yet everyone takes as zealous an interest in the affairs of his township, his county, and the whole State as if they were his own, because everyone, in his own sphere, takes an active part in the government of society.

The lower orders in the United States are aware of the influence that general prosperity has on their own welfare. Simple as this observation is, the people all too rarely make it. But in America the people regard this prosperity as the result of their own efforts. The citizen looks on the fortune of the public as his private interest, and he cooperates in its success, not so much from pride or from duty as from what I shall venture to call cupidity.

There is no need to study the institutions and the history of the Americans to see the truth of this remark, for their customs make it plain enough. Because the American takes part in everything done in his country, he thinks himself obliged to defend whatever is criticized. On these occasions it is not only his country that is attacked, but himself. The result is that his national pride resorts to a thousand artifices and to all the petty tricks of individual vanity.

Nothing is more embarrassing in the ordinary course of life than this irritable patriotism of the Americans. A stranger may be quite willing to praise many of the institutions of their country, but he asks permission to criticize some of the peculiarities he observes, and that permission is firmly refused. America is therefore a free country in which, lest anyone be hurt by your remarks, you are not allowed to speak freely of private individuals or of the state, of the citizens or of the authorities, of public or of private undertakings, or in short of anything at all, except the climate and the soil. And even then Americans will be found ready to defend one or the other, as if the inhabitants of the country had designed them.

In our times a choice must be made between the patriotism of all and the government of a few, for the force and activity that the first confers cannot be reconciled with the guarantees of tranquillity that the second provides.
Notion of Rights in the United States
No great people without a notion of rights—How the notion of rights can be given to a people—Respect for rights in the United States—Where it comes from.

After the idea of virtue, I know of no higher principle than that of right, or, to speak more precisely, these two ideas are blended into one. The idea of right is simply the idea of virtue brought into the political world. It is the idea of right that enabled men to define anarchy and tyranny, and that taught them to remain independent without arrogance and to obey without servility. The man who submits to violence is degraded by his compliance. But when he obeys the command of someone who holds that right of authority, which he acknowledges in a fellow creature, he rises in some measure above the person who gives the command. There are no great men without virtue, and there are no great nations without the notion of rights. It may almost be added that there would be no society at all without it, for what is the condition of a mass of rational and intelligent beings who are held together only by the bond of force?

I am convinced that the only means we now have of instilling the notion of rights, and of making it, as it were, palpable to the senses, is to give all members of the community the peaceful exercise of certain rights. This is very clearly seen in children, who are men without the strength and experience of manhood. When a child begins to move among the objects around him, he is instinctively led to turn everything he can lay his hands on to his own purposes. He has no notion of the property of others. But as he gradually learns the value of things and begins to see that he may in turn be deprived of his possessions, he becomes more cautious, and he respects in others the rights he wishes to have respected in himself. The principle that the child learns from possessing his toys is taught to the man by the things he can call his own. In America, the complaints against property in general that are so frequent in Europe are never heard, because in America there are no paupers. And since everyone has property of his own to defend, everyone recognizes the principle on which he holds it.

The same thing happens in the political world. In America the lowest classes have formed a very high notion of political rights, because they exercise those rights, and they refrain from attacking the rights of others so that their own will not be attacked. In Europe the same classes sometimes rebel even against the supreme power, while the American submits without a murmur to the authority of the pettiest magistrate.

This truth is shown in the most trivial details of national peculiarities. In France very few pleasures are kept for the higher classes alone. The poor are admitted wherever the rich are received, so they behave properly and respect whatever adds to the enjoyments they share. In England, where wealth monopolizes amusement as well as power, people complain that when the poor happen to sneak into the grounds set aside for the pleasures of the rich, they commit acts of wanton mischief. Is that surprising, when care has been taken that they should have nothing to lose? *b

b [ [This, too, has been remedied by much larger provisions for the amusements of the people in public parks, gardens, museums, and the like; and the conduct of the people in these places of amusement has improved in the same proportion.]]

The government of democracy brings the notion of political rights down to the level of the humblest citizens, just as the spread of wealth brings the notion of property within reach of all members of the community. I confess that, to my mind, this is one of its greatest advantages. I do not claim that it is easy to teach men to exercise political rights. But I maintain that when it can be done, the results are highly important, and I add that if there was ever a time when such an attempt should be made, that time is our own. It is clear that the influence of religious belief is shaken and that the notion of divine rights is declining. It is evident that public morality is corrupted and that the notion of moral rights is also disappearing. These are general signs of the replacement of faith by argument, and of the impulses of feeling by calculation. If, in the midst of this general breakdown, you do not succeed in connecting the notion of rights with that of personal interest, which is the only unchanging point in the human heart, what means will you have of governing the world except fear? I am told that, since the laws are weak and the populace is wild, since passions are excited and the authority of virtue is paralyzed, no measures should be taken to increase the rights of the democracy. I reply that it is for these very reasons that some measures of the kind must be taken. And I am convinced that governments have an even greater interest in taking them than society at large, because governments can be destroyed and society cannot perish.

I am not inclined, however, to exaggerate the example that America provides. In those States the people were given political rights at a time when those rights could scarcely be abused, for the citizens were few in number and simple in their customs. As they have multiplied, the Americans have not increased the power of the democracy, but they have, if I may use the expression, extended its dominions. There can be no doubt that the moment when political rights are granted to a people that had been without them is a very critical one, though a necessary one. A child may kill before he knows the value of life, and he may take another person’s property before he knows that his own can be taken from him. When the lower orders are first given political rights, they stand in relation to those rights as the child stands in relation to the whole of nature, and the famous adage may then be applied to them: Homo puer robustus. This truth can even be seen in America. The States where the citizens have enjoyed their rights longest are those where they make the best use of them.

It cannot be repeated too often that nothing is more productive of marvels than the art of being free, but nothing is harder than the apprenticeship of liberty. Despotic institutions are quite different. Despotism often promises to make up for a thousand earlier ills. It upholds the right, it protects the oppressed, and it maintains public order. The nation is lulled by the temporary prosperity that results, until it is roused to a sense of its own misery. Liberty, on the contrary, is generally established amid agitation, it is perfected by civil discord, and its benefits cannot be appreciated until it is already old.
Respect for the Law in the United States
Respect of the Americans for the law—The parental affection they feel for it—The personal interest of everyone in increasing the authority of the law.

It is not always possible to consult the whole people, directly or indirectly, in making the law. But it cannot be denied that when this is possible, the authority of the law is greatly increased. This popular origin, which lessens the excellence and wisdom of legislation, contributes enormously to its power. There is amazing strength in the expression of the determination of a whole people, and when it declares itself, the imagination of even those most inclined to resist it is overawed by its authority. Parties know this fact very well, and they therefore try to make out a majority whenever they can. If they do not have the greater number of voters on their side, they claim that the true majority abstained from voting. And if they are foiled even there, they turn to the body of those who had no votes to give.

In the United States, apart from slaves, servants, and paupers who receive relief from the townships, there is no class of persons who do not exercise the elective franchise and so contribute indirectly to making the laws. Those who intend to attack the laws must therefore either change the opinion of the nation or trample on its decision.

A second reason, still more weighty, may be added. In the United States everyone has a personal interest in enforcing the obedience of the whole community to the law. For the minority may soon win the majority over to its principles, and it therefore has an interest in professing the respect for the decrees of the legislator that it may soon need to claim for its own. However irksome an enactment may be, the citizen of the United States complies with it, not only because it is the work of the majority, but because it originates in his own authority, and he regards it as a contract to which he himself is a party.

In the United States, then, there is no numerous and turbulent multitude that always regards the law as its natural enemy and therefore looks on it with fear and distrust. On the other hand, it is impossible not to see that all classes show the utmost confidence in the legislation of their country and that they are attached to it by a kind of parental affection.

But I am wrong to say all classes, for in America the European scale of authority is inverted, and the wealthy are placed in a position like that of the poor in the Old World. It is the wealthy classes that often regard the law with suspicion. I have already observed that the advantage of democracy is not, as has sometimes been claimed, that it protects the interests of the whole community, but simply that it protects those of the majority. In the United States, where the poor rule, the rich always have some reason to fear the abuse of the poor’s power. This natural anxiety of the rich may produce a sullen dissatisfaction, but society is not disturbed by it. For the same reason that leads the rich to withhold their confidence from the legislative authority makes them obey its commands: their wealth, which prevents them from making the law, prevents them from resisting it. Among civilized nations, revolts are rarely stirred up except by people who have nothing to lose by them. And if the laws of a democracy are not always worthy of respect, at least they always obtain it. For those who usually break the laws have no excuse for not complying with enactments that they have made themselves and from which they benefit. Meanwhile the citizens whose interests might be served by breaking the laws are led, by their character and their position, to submit to the decisions of the legislature, whatever they may be. Besides, the people in America obey the law not only because it comes from the popular authority, but because that authority can change it in any point that proves vexatious. A law is obeyed because it is, first, an evil the people have imposed on themselves, and second, an evil of short duration.
Activity That Pervades All the Branches of the Body Politic in the United States; Influence It Exercises on Society

The political activity that pervades the United States is harder to imagine than the freedom and equality that reign there—The great activity that perpetually stirs the legislative bodies is only an episode in the general activity—It is difficult for an American to confine himself to his own business—Political agitation extends to all social intercourse—The commercial activity of the Americans is partly attributable to this cause—Indirect advantages that society derives from a democratic government.

When you pass from a country with free institutions to one where they do not exist, you are struck by the change. In the former all is bustle and activity, and in the latter everything is calm and motionless. In the one, improvement and progress are the general topics of inquiry. In the other, it seems as if the community aspired only to rest in the enjoyment of the advantages it has already gained. Nevertheless, the country that exerts itself so strenuously to promote its welfare is generally wealthier and more prosperous than the one that seems so content with its lot. And when we compare them, we can scarcely understand how so many new wants are felt every day in the first, while so few seem to arise in the second.

If this remark applies to those free countries in which monarchical and aristocratic institutions still exist, it is even more striking in democratic republics. In these States it is not just one part of the people that is busy improving its social condition. The whole community is engaged in the task, and provision is to be made not for the needs and convenience of a single class, but for the needs and convenience of all ranks of life.

It is not impossible to imagine the immense liberty the Americans enjoy, and some idea may also be formed of the extreme equality that exists among them. But the political activity that pervades the United States must be seen to be understood. No sooner do you set foot on American soil than you are stunned by a kind of tumult. A confused clamor rises on every side, and a thousand voices at once demand the immediate satisfaction of their social wants. Everything around you is in motion. Here, the people of one quarter of a town are meeting to decide on building a church. There, an election of a representative is under way. A little further on, the delegates of a district are hurrying to town to consult about some local improvements. In another place, the laborers of a village leave their plows to deliberate on a plan for a road or a public school. Meetings are called for the sole purpose of declaring disapproval of the government’s conduct, while in other assemblies the citizens hail the authorities of the day as the fathers of their country. Societies are formed that regard drunkenness as the principal cause of the evils from which the State suffers, and that solemnly bind themselves to set a constant example of temperance. *c

c [ While I was in the United States, the temperance societies already had more than 270,000 members. Their effect had been to cut the consumption of fermented liquors by 500,000 gallons a year in the State of Pennsylvania alone.]

The great political agitation of the American legislative bodies, which is the only kind of excitement that attracts the attention of foreign countries, is a mere episode, or a kind of continuation, of that universal movement which begins among the lowest classes of the people and spreads in turn to all ranks of society. It is impossible to put more effort into the pursuit of enjoyment.

The cares of political life take up a very prominent place in the occupations of a citizen of the United States, and almost the only pleasure an American can imagine is to take part in the government and to discuss the part he has taken. This feeling pervades even the most trifling habits of life. Even the women often attend public meetings and listen to political harangues as a recreation after their household labors. Debating clubs are, to a certain extent, a substitute for theatrical entertainments. An American cannot converse, but he can discuss, and when he tries to talk he falls into a lecture. He speaks to you as if he were addressing a meeting, and if he happens to grow warm in the course of the discussion, he will inevitably say “Gentlemen,” to the person he is talking with.

In some countries the inhabitants show a certain reluctance to use the political privileges with which the law invests them. It would seem that they set too high a value on their time to spend it on the interests of the community, and they prefer to withdraw within the exact limits of a wholesome egotism, marked out by four sunken fences and a quickset hedge. But if an American were condemned to confine his activity to his own affairs, he would be robbed of half his existence. He would feel an immense void in the life he is used to leading, and his wretchedness would be unbearable. *d I am convinced that if a despotic government is ever established in America, it will find it harder to overcome the habits that free institutions have produced than to conquer the citizens’ attachment to freedom.

d [ The same observation was made at Rome under the first Caesars. Somewhere Montesquieu mentions the excessive despondency of certain Roman citizens who, after the excitement of political life, were suddenly thrown back into the stagnation of private life.]
